rw: This cooling-off pause lets the first urge fade, so you can judge whether you truly need the item, can afford it, and want it a day later.

ww.The law requires a day's wait on all pur: No general law requires a one-day wait on purchases. The 24-hour rule is a personal habit people adopt, not a legal requirement set by the government.
ww.The price drops overnight, so waiting a: Prices do not reliably fall overnight, so waiting is not a way to save money. The benefit of the pause is better judgment, not a cheaper price tag.
ww.Stores must hold the item for free for a: Stores have no duty to hold an item for free for a day. Shelf stock can sell out, so the pause is for your decision, not for a store promise.

rw: As nonprofit, member-owned cooperatives, credit unions return earnings to members, so they often offer competitive savings rates and lower fees than many for-profit banks do.

ww.They are not insured, which raises the r: Credit unions are generally insured, by the NCUA up to set limits. Lack of insurance would add risk for savers and does not raise returns on deposits.
ww.They pay no interest, as credit unions a: Credit unions do pay interest, often called dividends, on member savings. Being a member-owned club does not mean the accounts earn nothing for their owners.
ww.They are open only to wealthy customers: Membership is based on a shared link such as employer, community or association, not on wealth. Many credit unions welcome ordinary savers with modest balances.

rw: A full-service broker provides personalized advice, planning and research along with executing trades. A discount broker mostly just executes the orders that clients place themselves.

ww.Lower commissions on every trade: Lower commissions are the mark of a discount broker. A full-service broker charges higher fees because it bundles in advice, research and personal attention for each client.
ww.No trading at all, only advice: Full-service brokers do trade for clients; they execute orders as well as give advice. Saying there is no trading at all describes an advisory-only service instead.
ww.Guaranteed returns on investments: No broker can guarantee investment returns, because every investment carries risk. A promise of guaranteed returns is a classic warning sign of fraud, not a service.

rw: A financial planner is a professional who helps clients set goals and build plans for saving, investing, insurance, taxes and retirement, based on their income and circumstances.

ww.A person who prepares meals in a restaur: Preparing meals for restaurant guests describes a cook or chef. A financial planner works with money goals and plans, not with food service in a kitchen.
ww.A person who sells cars at a dealership: Selling cars at a dealership describes a car salesperson. A financial planner does not sell vehicles, and gives advice on money matters instead of vehicle sales.
ww.A person who collects taxes for the gove: Collecting taxes at a border post describes a customs officer working for the government. A financial planner advises private clients and does not collect any taxes for the state.

rw: The SEC adviser search and FINRA BrokerCheck databases list registered advisers and brokers, along with their licenses and any disciplinary history, so you can verify them yourself for free.

ww.Count their social media followers: Social media follower counts measure popularity, not credentials. Scammers can buy followers, so a large following says nothing about whether an adviser is registered or trustworthy.
ww.Ask the adviser if they are honest: An adviser who is dishonest will simply say yes, so asking proves nothing. Registration must be checked with an independent official source, not with the adviser's own words.
ww.Look at the adviser's car and office: A fancy car or office shows spending, not legitimacy. Fraudsters often use a polished image to win trust, so appearance cannot confirm that an adviser is registered.

rw: A payday lender makes small, short-term loans with high fees that come due on the borrower's next payday, which often leads to costly rollovers and a cycle of debt.

ww.A bank that pays its workers on the same: Paying workers on a fixed monthly date is just payroll, which any employer does. A payday lender is a business that makes loans, not a bank that issues wages.
ww.A lender offering long-term, low-cost lo: Long-term, low-cost home loans repaid over thirty years are mortgages. Payday loans are the opposite, being very short and very expensive, so this describes the wrong product.
ww.A government agency that lends money to: A government agency lending to students describes federal student loans. Payday lenders are private businesses that charge high fees on short loans, not a public education agency.

rw: The fee is 45 divided by 300, or 15 percent per two weeks. With 26 two-week terms in a year, 15 times 26 is 390 percent APR.

ww.About 45 percent: A $45 fee on $300 is 15 percent for just two weeks, not 45 percent. The 45 is the dollar fee, and the yearly rate must be scaled up.
ww.About 15 percent: The fee is 15 percent of the loan, but that covers only two weeks. Stopping there ignores the annual rate, which requires multiplying by the 26 periods in a year.
ww.About 30 percent: Thirty percent would double the true two-week cost. The actual fee is 15 percent of $300, and annualizing it gives far more than 30 percent, namely about 390 percent.

rw: A title loan is a short-term, high-cost loan secured by the borrower's vehicle title. If the borrower cannot repay, the lender can repossess the car or truck.

ww.A loan that is given to students with no: Student loans are not title loans, and a title loan is not unsecured. It requires collateral in the form of a vehicle, not borrowers with no collateral at all.
ww.A loan secured by a house and repaid ove: A loan secured by a house and repaid over decades is a mortgage. Title loans use a vehicle as collateral and are due within weeks or months.
ww.A loan that is repaid in one year with n: Title loans are not interest free. They carry high fees and interest, are due in a short time, and risk losing the vehicle if the borrower fails to repay.

rw: An insurance agent sells policies, explains the terms and costs, and helps customers choose coverage that fits their needs, such as auto, home, life or health protection.

ww.Collects income taxes from people and bu: Collecting income taxes for the government is the job of tax authorities like the IRS. An insurance agent works in the private insurance business and has no role in collecting taxes.
ww.Invests customers' money in the stock ma: Investing customers' money in the stock market is the job of a broker or investment adviser. An insurance agent sells protection against loss and does not manage investments.
ww.Lends money to customers for homes and c: Lending money for homes and cars is done by banks and other lenders. An insurance agent sells policies and does not make loans to customers.

rw: A tax preparer helps individuals and businesses complete and file their tax returns, using their income records and applicable rules to calculate what is owed or refunded.

ww.A person who audits government agencies: Auditing government agencies is the work of government auditors. A tax preparer assists private clients with returns and does not examine public bodies in this way.
ww.A person who sets tax rates for the coun: Governments, not preparers, set tax rates and collect taxes. A tax preparer only helps people file returns under the rates that lawmakers have already chosen.
ww.A person who collects taxes at the borde: Collecting taxes at a border crossing is the job of customs officers. A tax preparer helps people complete returns and has no authority to collect duties.

rw: An Enrolled Agent is a tax expert licensed by the IRS who can prepare returns and represent taxpayers before the IRS in audits, appeals and collection matters.

ww.Auditing public companies and signing th: Auditing public companies and signing their reports is the work of a certified public accountant. Enrolled agents focus on taxes, not on audits of company financial statements.
ww.Selling insurance policies to families a: Selling insurance policies is the work of insurance agents and brokers. Enrolled agents are federally licensed tax professionals, not insurance salespeople for families and firms.
ww.Planning retirement savings for clients: Retirement planning is the work of financial planners. An enrolled agent specializes in taxes and is licensed by the IRS, not in building savings plans for retirement.

rw: A robo-advisor is an online service that uses algorithms to build and manage a diversified portfolio for clients, usually at a low cost and with little human input.

ww.A machine that prints stock certificates: Printing stock certificates is a job for printers and transfer agents. A robo-advisor is software that manages investments, not a machine that produces paper certificates for companies.
ww.A robot that works in a bank branch hand: Despite the name, a robo-advisor is software and not a physical robot. It runs on algorithms, not by handling cash for staff inside a bank branch.
ww.A human financial planner who meets clie: A human planner who meets clients in person is the traditional model. A robo-advisor is the opposite, being automated and online instead of a person meeting clients monthly.

rw: A mortgage broker is an intermediary who compares loan offers from many lenders and helps borrowers find and apply for a home loan with suitable rates and terms.

ww.A person who sells homes for owners in t: Selling homes for owners is the work of a real estate agent. A mortgage broker deals with loans, not with listing or marketing houses for sale.
ww.A person who sets the interest rate on a: Banks and lenders set loan interest rates, based on market conditions and the borrower's risk. A broker only shops for rates and does not set them.
ww.A person who inspects homes for defects: Inspecting homes for defects is done by a home inspector. A mortgage broker deals with financing and does not examine the physical condition of a property.

rw: The insurer pays the repair cost minus the deductible: $2,500 minus $500 equals $2,000. You pay the first $500 and the insurer covers the remaining amount.

ww.$500: The $500 is what you pay as the deductible, not what the insurer pays. The insurer pays the remainder of the bill, which is $2,000.
ww.$2,500: Paying the full $2,500 would ignore the deductible. Because you must first cover $500 yourself, the insurer's share is $2,500 minus $500, which is $2,000.
ww.$3,000: A payout of $3,000 exceeds the entire $2,500 repair bill, so it is impossible. The insurer pays $2,500 minus the $500 deductible, which equals $2,000.

rw: A higher deductible means you pay more of each loss yourself, so the insurer takes less risk and charges a lower premium. You should keep savings to cover it.

ww.Choosing a lower deductible: A lower deductible means the insurer pays more of each claim, so it charges a higher premium. Choosing it raises your cost and does not lower it.
ww.Adding more coverage than needed: More coverage than needed means the insurer takes on more risk, so the premium goes up. Paying for extra protection you do not need raises your cost.
ww.Filing many small claims yearly: Filing many small claims marks you as a higher risk, so insurers usually raise premiums or may even drop you. Frequent claims push your costs up.

rw: Renters insurance covers the tenant's personal belongings against events like fire and theft, plus liability if someone is hurt, but it does not cover the building itself.

ww.It pays the rent when the tenant loses a: Renters insurance does not pay rent when a tenant loses a job. It protects belongings and liability, and only some policies add limited living costs after a covered loss.
ww.It pays for repairs to the landlord's pi: Repairs to the landlord's pipes and roof are the landlord's responsibility, covered by the landlord's own policy. Renters insurance does not insure the building structure.
ww.It covers the building and the land on w: Covering the building and land is the job of the owner's homeowners policy. A tenant does not own the structure, so renters insurance does not insure it.

rw: Standard homeowners policies usually exclude flood damage, so owners must buy separate flood insurance, such as through the National Flood Insurance Program, to be protected from rising water.

ww.Floods are always covered in standard po: Standard homeowners policies typically exclude flood damage. They are not always covered, and flood protection costs extra, so this claim is false and could mislead owners.
ww.The insurer must pay for it under any po: Insurers pay only for losses covered by the policy terms. Exclusions are legal and common, so the insurer need not pay for floods under a standard policy.
ww.The owner cannot file claims, as insurer: Owners can still file claims, and insurers do pay for many water losses such as burst pipes. Only flood from rising water is usually excluded from a standard policy.

rw: Life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries, so it replaces lost income and covers debts and expenses for dependents if the insured person dies.

ww.To provide income for the insured while: Life insurance pays out when the insured dies, not while healthy. Providing income during working years is the purpose of disability insurance, not a life policy.
ww.To pay for a house and the land it sits: Buying a home is financed with a mortgage and savings. Life insurance does not pay for a house and land while the insured is alive.
ww.To pay medical bills of the insured pers: Medical bills of the insured person are covered by health insurance. Life insurance pays only after death, to the beneficiaries, and not for medical costs.

rw: With no dependents to support and few debts, no one relies on the person's income, so little or no life insurance is needed beyond funeral and final expenses.

ww.Whole life with a large cash value for l: Whole life with a large cash value is costly and suits specific needs. A single person with no dependents has little reason to pay for it.
ww.A policy worth ten times the person's in: Ten times income is a rule of thumb for families with dependents and debts. A single person with no dependents and few debts does not need that much.
ww.The most costly policy, for single peopl: The most costly policy wastes money for someone with no dependents. Insurance should match real financial needs, and this person has few needs to cover.

rw: Insurers price by risk, and statistics show inexperienced young drivers have more accidents. Higher expected claims for this group lead to higher premiums until experience builds up.

ww.Young drivers drive newer cars only, whi: Young drivers often drive older, cheaper cars. Newer cars would not explain the higher premiums, since the main driver of price is higher accident risk based on data.
ww.Young drivers are never insured, as firm: Young drivers can be insured, and most are, often on a parent's policy. Insurers charge more for them instead of refusing, because the law and market allow pricing by risk.
ww.Young drivers always cause accidents on: Young drivers do not cause accidents on purpose. Their higher premiums come from inexperience and statistics, not from any intent to crash, which would also be fraud.

rw: Gap insurance pays the difference between a car's current value and the amount still owed on its loan or lease when the car is totaled or stolen.

ww.Coverage for gaps between two insurance: Gap insurance is not about holding two policies in sequence. It is tied to a vehicle loan, and its purpose is to cover a shortfall in value.
ww.Coverage for the gap between rich and po: The gap between rich and poor is a social idea, not an insurance product. Gap insurance is a car coverage with a specific financial purpose.
ww.Coverage for gaps in your schedule when: Gaps in your schedule or commute are not covered by any such policy. Gap insurance is about loan balance versus car value after a total loss.

rw: Gap insurance covers the difference between what you owe and what the car is worth. Here that is $18,000 minus $14,000, which is exactly the $4,000 shortfall.

ww.Renters insurance: Renters insurance covers belongings and liability for tenants. It has no connection to a car loan balance and would not pay any part of the $4,000 shortfall.
ww.Disability cover: Disability cover replaces income when you cannot work due to illness or injury. It does not pay car loan shortfalls after a vehicle is totaled.
ww.Travel insurance: Travel insurance covers trip problems such as cancellations and medical care abroad. It does not pay the difference between a totaled car's value and the loan balance.

rw: A home inventory is a list, often with photos or video, of your belongings and their estimated values. It documents what you own so a claim can be proven.

ww.A list of home repair tools kept in the: Tools kept in the garage are only a small part of a household's belongings. A home inventory lists all possessions, not just items used for repairs.
ww.A list of rooms in the house and their s: A list of rooms and their sizes describes the home's layout. A home inventory records the contents and their values, which is what insurers need for claims.
ww.A list of bills paid in a year by the ho: A list of bills paid is a budget or expense record. A home inventory records possessions and their values, not household payments made during the year.

rw: After a fire, an inventory with photos and values documents what you owned, so you can file a complete claim faster and prove the amounts you ask for.

ww.It prevents fire, as the insurer sees a: An inventory does not prevent fires, and insurers do not judge a home as safe from it. Its value comes after a loss, in documenting what was lost.
ww.It is needed only for the tax return fil: An inventory is useful for insurance claims, not only for taxes. Its main purpose after a fire is documenting lost belongings, though it may help with casualty losses too.
ww.It lowers the deductible for the claim m: Your deductible is set in the policy and an inventory does not change it. The list only supports the value of your claim and does not cut what you pay.

rw: An adjuster investigates a reported loss, inspects damage, reviews the policy and decides how much the insurer should pay on the claim, acting for the insurance company.

ww.Collects premium payments from all polic: Collecting premiums is handled by billing staff or agents of the insurer. An adjuster works after a loss, on the claims side, and not on premium payments.
ww.Sets the premium for each customer in th: Setting premiums is the job of underwriters and actuaries, who assess risk before a policy is issued. An adjuster deals with claims after a loss instead.
ww.Sells policies to new customers on behal: Selling policies is the work of agents and brokers. An adjuster does not market coverage but evaluates claims after a loss has occurred and decides on payment.

rw: An underwriter evaluates an applicant's risk, then decides whether the insurer will issue a policy and what premium to charge, using factors like health, driving record or property.

ww.Investigates claims after a loss and dec: Investigating claims after a loss and deciding payouts is the job of a claims adjuster. An underwriter works earlier, evaluating risk before a policy is issued.
ww.Sells policies to the public and keeps t: Selling policies to the public is the work of agents. Underwriters work inside the insurer, judging whether to accept an applicant, and do not sell policies.
ww.Checks the financial statements of the i: Checking the insurer's financial statements for errors is the work of auditors and accountants. An underwriter evaluates applicants' risk and not the insurer's own books.

rw: A rider is an add-on to a base policy that extends or changes coverage for a specific item or risk, such as jewelry or accidental death, usually for extra cost.

ww.A driver who is named on a car policy as: A driver named on a car policy is a listed driver, not a rider. A rider is an attached provision that adds coverage to an existing policy.
ww.A person who files claims with the insur: A person who files claims for the holder is a claimant or representative. A rider is a policy provision, not a person, and it extends coverage.
ww.A discount for good behavior by the poli: A discount for good behavior is a premium credit. A rider adds coverage and generally increases cost, rather than lowering the premium for safe habits.

rw: A beneficiary is the person or entity named to receive the proceeds of a life insurance policy or account when the owner dies, without needing to go through probate.

ww.The person who sells the policy to the c: The person who sells the policy is an agent or broker. A beneficiary is named by the policyholder to receive the proceeds, and does not sell anything.
ww.The person who investigates the claim af: Investigating a claim is the job of an adjuster. A beneficiary is simply the person named to receive benefits and does not examine any loss.
ww.The person who pays the premium on an in: Paying the premium is the duty of the policyholder or owner. A beneficiary receives the benefit and need not pay the premiums on the policy.

rw: Going uninsured means paying all costs yourself. Saving $300 a month is small compared with a $40,000 bill, which shows how a single event can outweigh years of savings.

ww.Paying low premiums: Low premiums are not the danger here. The risk is having no coverage, since the person saved $300 a month but then faced a $40,000 bill alone.
ww.A low deductible: A low deductible would have limited the person's own share of the bill. The person had no insurance at all, so no deductible applied to the $40,000.
ww.Too much cover: Having too much cover is the opposite of this case. The person bought none, and the large hospital bill shows how costly being underinsured can be.

rw: Marriage changes needs, such as dependents, shared property and income, so reviewing coverage keeps it adequate, avoids gaps and may reveal savings or better beneficiary choices.

ww.Policies update by themselves: Policies do not update themselves after marriage. The policyholder must contact the insurer to change names, beneficiaries, coverage amounts or drivers on the policy.
ww.Rates drop after every marriage: Rates do not automatically drop after marriage. Some insurers offer discounts, but nothing guarantees lower rates, so the review should focus on needs and risks instead.
ww.Policies lapse when a person marries: Policies do not lapse just because the holder marries. They stay in force while premiums are paid, though details like beneficiaries may need updating after the change.

rw: Long-term care insurance pays for extended help with daily living, such as nursing home or in-home care, which regular health insurance and Medicare often cover little or not at all.

ww.The cost of a car repair after any traff: Car repairs after a traffic accident are paid under auto insurance. Long-term care insurance is meant for personal care over an extended time due to age or illness.
ww.The cost of a short hospital stay for a: A short hospital stay for a minor operation is covered by health insurance. Long-term care is for extended care needs over months or years, not brief treatment.
ww.The cost of routine doctor visits and ch: Routine visits and checkups are paid by regular health insurance. Long-term care insurance focuses on extended custodial and nursing care, not everyday doctor appointments.

rw: Safety steps such as smoke detectors, seat belts or helmets reduce how likely a loss is or how bad it gets, which is the definition of risk reduction.

ww.Risk retention: Retention means accepting a risk and paying for any loss yourself, often from savings. Safety steps aim to lessen the chance of loss and do not simply accept it.
ww.Risk avoidance: Avoidance means staying away from the risky activity entirely. Safety steps keep you doing the activity but with lower risk, so this is not avoidance.
ww.Risk transfer: Transfer shifts the financial cost to another party, such as an insurer. Safety steps cut the chance of loss directly and do not move the cost to anyone.

rw: Buying insurance shifts the financial cost of a possible loss to the insurer in return for premiums, which is the textbook example of risk transfer.

ww.Risk avoidance: Avoidance means not doing the risky activity at all. Buying a policy keeps you in the activity and shifts the financial cost to another party instead.
ww.Risk retention: Retention means you absorb the loss yourself. Buying insurance does the opposite, passing the cost of a possible loss to the insurer in exchange for a premium.
ww.Risk reduction: Reduction lowers the chance or size of a loss through safety steps. Buying a policy does not change how likely the loss is, only who pays.

rw: Avoiding the activity entirely, so that no motorcycle accident can ever happen to you, is risk avoidance. You eliminate exposure instead of managing or paying for it.

ww.Risk reduction: Risk reduction means keeping the activity but lowering the danger, as with a helmet. Choosing not to ride at all removes the activity completely, which is avoidance.
ww.Risk transfer: Transfer shifts the cost of a loss to someone else, like an insurer. Not riding a motorcycle shifts nothing; it simply removes the risky activity from your life.
ww.Risk retention: Retention means you keep the risk and accept possible loss. Declining to ride removes the exposure entirely, so you are not retaining the motorcycle risk.

rw: Setting aside savings to pay for small repairs yourself means you keep the risk and cover the loss from your own funds, which is risk retention.

ww.Risk transfer: Transfer moves the cost to another party such as an insurer. Setting aside your own savings keeps the cost with you, so it is not transfer.
ww.Risk avoidance: Avoidance means not doing the risky activity. Saving for repairs means you still own the item and accept possible costs, so you have not avoided anything.
ww.Risk reduction: Reduction lowers the chance or size of loss through actions like maintenance. A savings fund only pays for repairs after they happen, so it does not reduce risk.

rw: A small cost you can easily pay from savings is best retained, because insurance premiums and paperwork would cost more than the likely loss. Insure only large risks.

ww.A lawsuit from a crash that hurts many p: A lawsuit from a crash that hurts many people could be enormous and ruin you financially. Such a large liability should be transferred through liability insurance, not retained.
ww.A huge medical bill far too large for sa: A huge medical bill far beyond your savings is a catastrophic loss. It is the type of risk that should be insured rather than retained.
ww.A house fire that destroys the whole hom: A house fire that destroys the whole home is a severe loss that few households can afford alone. It should be insured and not retained.

rw: If the company fails, you could lose both your paycheck and your investment at once. Holding too much employer stock ties your income and savings to one firm.

ww.Employer stock cannot lose value over a: Employer stock can lose value, as shown by company failures. Holding too much of it concentrates risk, so it can fall sharply when the company struggles.
ww.Employers ban employees from selling it: Employees are generally allowed to sell their employer stock, aside from limited trading windows or vesting rules. A ban is not why holding too much is risky.
ww.Employer stock pays a lower dividend tha: Dividend level is not the main concern, since some employers pay generous dividends. The real danger is concentrating both income and savings in one company.

rw: Working smoke detectors give early warning and watching the stove prevents cooking fires, which are a leading cause of home fires, so both actions reduce risk.

ww.Storing gasoline cans in the house near: Storing gasoline near a heating unit creates a serious fire hazard because fumes can ignite. This raises the risk of a home fire instead of reducing it.
ww.Overloading electrical outlets with many: Overloading outlets can overheat wiring and start electrical fires. It is a known hazard that increases fire risk and so does not reduce it.
ww.Leaving candles burning while you sleep: Candles left burning while you sleep can tip over or ignite nearby items with nobody awake to react. This raises fire risk and does not reduce it.

rw: A safe deposit box is a secure bank vault compartment for important documents, such as deeds and wills, and valuables like jewelry, which are hard or costly to replace.

ww.Hiding your passwords on a note card: Hiding passwords on a note card in a deposit box adds little, and it is not the box's main purpose. The box protects documents and valuables, which are hard to replace.
ww.Keeping everyday spending money in it: Everyday spending money should be easy to reach, and a safe deposit box has limited bank hours. It suits irreplaceable items and not cash used daily.
ww.Storing perishable food and drinks in it: Perishable food and drinks would spoil in a sealed metal box, and banks do not allow it. The box is for documents and valuables, not groceries.

rw: Strong, unique passwords stop one breach from spreading to other accounts, and multi-factor authentication adds a second barrier, so together they sharply cut the chance of identity theft.

ww.Click links in emails to check that acco: Clicking links in emails is how phishing works, because fake sites steal logins. To check an account safely, go to the official site directly instead.
ww.Share passwords with friends so they can: Sharing passwords gives others access to your accounts and may lead to theft or misuse. Passwords should be kept private, and friends cannot warn you reliably.
ww.Use one simple password everywhere so th: Using one simple password everywhere means one leak exposes every account. Simple passwords are also easy to guess, so this practice raises the risk of identity theft.

rw: An emergency fund pays for surprises like car repairs or lost income from cash on hand, so you avoid debt and high-interest borrowing, which reduces financial risk.

ww.It earns the highest return of any asset: An emergency fund is kept in safe, easy-access savings, so it earns modest interest. It is not meant to earn the highest return, since its job is protection.
ww.It guarantees that no emergency will occ: No fund can guarantee that emergencies will not occur. It only prepares you to handle them financially when they do happen, so the guarantee claim is false.
ww.It replaces all insurance as a fund pays: An emergency fund cannot replace insurance, because a large loss such as a house fire or major illness would exhaust it quickly. It complements coverage and does not substitute for it.

rw: Spreading money across many investments means a poor result in any one has a limited effect on the whole portfolio, which reduces the risk tied to a single holding.

ww.The risk that taxes are too low for save: Diversification does not control tax levels. Tax rates are set by law, and spreading investments does not make taxes lower or higher for savers.
ww.The risk that market prices rise too qui: Diversification does not control how fast market prices rise. It protects against falling values in one holding and does not manage rising market prices.
ww.The risk that inflation is too low for i: Diversification does not affect the inflation rate. Inflation is a broad economic force, and spreading holdings cannot change it, though it may help returns overall.

rw: Year one gives $1,000 times 1.05, or $1,050. Year two gives $1,050 times 1.05, which is $1,102.50, because interest is earned on the first year's interest too.

ww.$1,100: At 5 percent simple, $1,000 would reach only $1,100 after two years. Compounding earns interest on interest, so the second year adds $52.50 and not $50.
ww.$1,250: A total of $1,250 would need 25 percent growth. Two years at 5 percent adds about 10.25 percent in total, which gives $1,102.50 and not $1,250.
ww.$1,050: $1,050 is the balance after only one year of 5 percent interest. The question asks about two years, so the money grows again to $1,102.50.

rw: Simple interest is $5,000 times 0.04 times 3, which is $600. Adding the $5,000 principal gives a total of $5,600 after three years.

ww.$600: $600 is only the interest earned: $5,000 times 0.04 times 3 years. The question asks for the total balance, which adds back the original $5,000 principal.
ww.$6,000: $6,000 would need 20 percent total interest, or about 6.7 percent a year. At 4 percent simple for 3 years the interest is $600, so the total is $5,600.
ww.$5,200: $5,200 is the balance after just one year, $5,000 plus $200 of interest. After three years the interest is $600, so the total is $5,600.

rw: Each share gained $6 because $26 minus $20 is $6. Multiplying by 50 shares gives a gain of $300, ignoring fees.

ww.$1,300: $1,300 is the total sale value, 50 times $26. It is not the gain, since you must subtract the $1,000 cost to find the $300 profit.
ww.$1,000: $1,000 is what you paid for the shares, 50 times $20. The gain is the difference between sale value and cost, which is $300.
ww.$6: $6 is the gain on a single share. With 50 shares, you multiply the per-share gain by 50, which gives $300 in total.

rw: Dividend income equals the per-share dividend times the number of shares, so $1.50 times 200 shares equals $300 received in total.

ww.$133: $133 has no basis in the numbers given. Dividend income is the per-share dividend times shares owned, so $1.50 times 200 gives $300.
ww.$1.50: $1.50 is the dividend for one share only. You own 200 shares, so you multiply $1.50 by 200 and receive $300 in total.
ww.$201.50: $201.50 comes from adding 200 and 1.50, which is the wrong operation. Dividends scale with the number of shares, so you multiply and get $300.

rw: The gain is $12,000 minus $10,000, or $2,000. Dividing by the original $10,000 gives 0.20, so the total increase over two years is 20 percent.

ww.16.7 percent: 16.7 percent divides the $2,000 gain by the new value of $12,000. Percent increase must be measured against the starting amount of $10,000, which gives 20 percent.
ww.12 percent: 12 percent just copies the digits of $12,000. The increase is $2,000 on a $10,000 start, and $2,000 divided by $10,000 is 20 percent.
ww.2 percent: 2 percent confuses the two years with a percentage. The actual gain of $2,000 on $10,000 is 20 percent in total, or roughly 9.5 percent per year compounded.

rw: A savings or checking account lets you withdraw quickly without penalty and is usually insured, so it is the best place for money you may need within days.

ww.A five-year CD with a penalty for early: A five-year CD charges a penalty for early withdrawal, which makes it a poor home for money you might need within days. Access matters most here.
ww.A long-term retirement fund of stocks an: Retirement funds of stocks and bonds are meant for decades and can fall in value. Early withdrawal also brings penalties, which makes them unsuitable for near-term needs.
ww.A single speculative stock that may fall: A single speculative stock can drop sharply in just a few days. Money needed soon should never be exposed to that much risk, so it is unsuitable.

rw: Keeping savings in a separate account puts a small barrier between you and the money, so you are less tempted to spend it on impulse and the balance can grow.

ww.It removes the need to budget at all: Separate accounts do not remove the need to budget. A budget is still how you plan income and spending, and the account is only one tool within it.
ww.It prevents all deposits from being made: A separate savings account does not stop deposits. You can still deposit into it, and it is simply set apart from daily spending money.
ww.It guarantees higher interest at banks: Interest rates depend on the bank and the account type, and nothing guarantees a higher rate just by separating savings. The real benefit is less temptation to spend.

rw: A CD locks your money for a fixed term, so withdrawing early usually triggers a penalty, often some months of interest. That lack of flexibility is its main drawback.

ww.It pays no interest during the term: CDs do pay interest during the term, usually at a fixed rate that is higher than ordinary savings. Paying nothing is not a drawback that applies.
ww.It loses all value in the term: CDs do not lose their value during the term. Deposits are normally insured up to limits and the principal is safe, so total loss is not a real drawback.
ww.It has no insurance of any kind: CDs at insured banks and credit unions are protected by FDIC or NCUA insurance up to set limits. Having no insurance of any kind is therefore not true.

rw: The difference is 4 percent minus 1 percent, or 3 percentage points. Three percent of $10,000 is $300, so the higher account pays about $300 more in one year.

ww.$30: $30 would be the gap if the rates were 0.1 and 0.4 percent. The gap here is 3 percentage points on $10,000, which gives $300.
ww.$500: $500 would require a 5 percentage point gap, such as 1 percent against 6 percent. The real gap is 3 points, and 3 percent of $10,000 is $300.
ww.$3,000: $3,000 would be a 30 percent difference in rates. The gap here is only 3 percentage points, and 3 percent of $10,000 comes to $300.

rw: An automatic transfer moves money to savings on a schedule, so you save steadily without having to remember or decide each time, which takes willpower out of the process.

ww.It removes the need for any bank account: Automatic transfers move money between accounts, so you still need bank accounts, including one to send from and one to receive the savings. They do not remove accounts.
ww.It allows spending of saved money at any: Automatic transfers are for building savings, and saved money should not be spent freely. The feature does not control spending, and its aim is steady saving.
ww.It earns the highest interest in the mar: Interest rates depend on the account, not on how deposits arrive. An automatic transfer does not earn the highest market rate, and no method guarantees that.

rw: Buy and hold means purchasing investments and keeping them for many years, riding out ups and downs, which avoids frequent trading costs and taxes and favors long-term growth.

ww.Buying and selling every day to gain fro: Buying and selling every day to gain from small price moves is day trading, which is the opposite of buy and hold and adds costs and risk.
ww.Buying only when prices fall and selling: Buying when prices fall and selling when they rise describes market timing. Buy and hold does not try to time the market and simply stays invested.
ww.Buying investments with borrowed money a: Buying with borrowed money and selling soon is margin trading for short-term gain. Buy and hold uses your own money and keeps the investment for the long term.

rw: For a goal one year away, safety and easy access matter most, so savings accounts or short-term CDs protect the principal and still earn some interest.

ww.All in a start-up business that has no r: A start-up with no revenue is extremely risky and could lose everything within the year. A goal only one year away needs safety of principal, not speculation.
ww.All in a single speculative stock held f: A single speculative stock can fall sharply in one year, and there is little time to recover. A one-year goal calls for safer and more stable choices.
ww.All in a long-term growth fund that may: Long-term growth funds can lose value in any given year, and one year is too short to recover from a drop. They suit goals many years away.

rw: Extra payments reduce the principal faster, so less interest accrues each month. The loan is paid off sooner and the total interest cost falls.

ww.Interest is unchanged, extra payments do: Extra payments do help. They cut the principal, and since interest is charged on the remaining balance, a smaller balance means less interest is owed.
ww.You pay more interest, as the balance fa: Extra payments make the balance fall faster, not slower, so you pay less interest overall. Claiming that interest rises gets the effect backwards.
ww.The loan is canceled at once by the bank: Extra payments do not cancel a loan at once. The bank only applies them to reduce what you owe, and the loan ends when the balance reaches zero.

rw: A prepayment penalty is a fee some lenders charge when you pay off all or part of a loan early, because they lose the interest they expected to earn.

ww.A fine for paying late on a monthly bill: A fine for paying late is a late fee. A prepayment penalty is the opposite situation, charged when you pay off a loan too early, not too late.
ww.A tax on loans paid to the state by a le: A tax paid to the state by a lender is not a prepayment penalty. This fee is charged to the borrower by the lender for early payoff.
ww.A reward for paying early on a loan from: Lenders do not reward early payment with this term. A prepayment penalty is a cost to the borrower, not a reward, so this has the meaning reversed.

rw: An I bond is a U.S. savings bond whose interest combines a fixed rate and an inflation rate, so its value keeps pace with rising prices and protects buying power.

ww.A bond that pays a fixed rate for thirty: A bond paying a fixed rate for thirty years describes a long-term Treasury bond. An I bond differs because its rate adjusts with inflation, not staying fixed.
ww.A bond issued by a company to fund its f: A bond issued by a company to fund factories is a corporate bond. An I bond is a savings bond issued by the U.S. Treasury, not a business.
ww.A bond issued by a foreign government to: Bonds issued by a foreign government to raise funds are foreign sovereign bonds. An I bond is issued by the U.S. government, not by another country.

rw: Roth IRA contributions are made with after-tax money, so qualified withdrawals in retirement, including the growth, are tax-free. This is the main reason people choose it.

ww.It can be opened only by retirees over s: Roth IRAs are open to workers of any age who have earned income and meet the income limits. They are not restricted to retirees over sixty.
ww.Contributions are deductible, withdrawal: This describes a traditional IRA, where contributions may be deductible and withdrawals are taxed. Roth contributions are made after tax, so that is the opposite.
ww.It has no contribution limits at all for: Roth IRAs do have contribution limits, set yearly by law, plus income limits for eligibility. Saying there are no limits at all is false.

rw: The standard rule lets people withdraw from an IRA without the 10 percent early-withdrawal penalty once they reach age 59 and a half, though ordinary income tax may apply.

ww.40: Age 40 is far too early. Withdrawals before 59 and a half generally trigger a 10 percent penalty plus income tax, unless a special exception applies.
ww.50: Age 50 is still before 59 and a half, so a withdrawal would normally face the 10 percent early-withdrawal penalty unless an exception applies.
ww.70: Age 70 is later than needed. The penalty ends at 59 and a half, though required withdrawals eventually begin in the seventies for most people.

rw: An RMD is the minimum amount you must withdraw each year from certain retirement accounts, like traditional IRAs, once you reach a set age, so that tax-deferred money eventually gets taxed.

ww.The fee charged to withdraw funds early: The fee charged for early withdrawal is the early-withdrawal penalty, usually 10 percent. An RMD is a mandatory withdrawal later in life, not a penalty fee.
ww.The maximum amount that may be withdrawn: An RMD is a minimum that must be withdrawn, not a maximum cap. You may withdraw more than the required amount, so the maximum description is wrong.
ww.The smallest deposit allowed in a retire: An RMD relates to withdrawals, not deposits. The smallest deposit allowed is a different matter set by the plan, while an RMD forces money out of the account.

rw: Social Security is a federal program funded by payroll taxes that pays monthly retirement, disability and survivor benefits to eligible workers and their families.

ww.A loan program for homebuyers who are fi: Loans for first-time homebuyers are offered by lenders and housing agencies. Social Security is a benefits program funded by payroll taxes and is not a loan program.
ww.A private savings account that each work: Social Security is not a private account. It is a government program funded by current payroll taxes, and workers do not own individual balances in it.
ww.A tax on investment gains and capital sa: A tax on investment gains is a capital gains tax. Social Security is funded by payroll taxes and pays benefits instead of taxing investments.

rw: Benefits typically replace only about 40 percent of pre-retirement earnings for an average worker, so people also need personal savings, pensions or retirement accounts to maintain their lifestyle.

ww.It is paid to every citizen at 18 years: Social Security is not paid to everyone at 18. Benefits depend on work history and age, and retirement benefits start no earlier than 62.
ww.It is a private account that grows fast,: Social Security is a government program, not a private account, and its benefits are modest. They are meant to supplement other savings and not fully cover expenses.
ww.It pays more than a worker's final salar: Benefits are based on past earnings and are almost always lower than a final salary. Saying it pays more in all cases is false.

rw: Total deductions are $200 plus $153 plus $60, which is $413. Subtracting from $2,000 gives a net pay of $1,587.

ww.$2,413: $2,413 would be gross pay plus the deductions, which adds when it should subtract. Net pay is gross pay minus every tax withheld from the check.
ww.$1,800: $1,800 subtracts only the federal tax of $200 and ignores FICA and state tax. Net pay must subtract all three deductions from gross pay.
ww.$413: $413 is the total of the deductions, not the pay. Net pay is what remains after subtracting them from $2,000, which is $1,587.

rw: The employee share is 7.65 percent of $2,000, and $2,000 times 0.0765 equals $153. That amount is withheld for Social Security and Medicare.

ww.$15.30: $15.30 comes from a misplaced decimal, using 0.765 percent instead of 7.65 percent. The correct calculation, $2,000 times 0.0765, gives $153.
ww.$765: $765 would be 38.25 percent of $2,000. FICA is 7.65 percent of pay, so the withholding is $153 and not $765.
ww.$1,847: $1,847 is the pay left after FICA, which is $2,000 minus $153. The question asks how much is withheld, and that is $153.

rw: FICA taxes are payroll taxes that fund Social Security, which pays retirement, disability and survivor benefits, and Medicare, which provides health coverage mainly for people age 65 and older.

ww.Highway and road construction: Highways and roads are paid mainly from fuel taxes and general funds. FICA taxes are dedicated payroll taxes with different purposes.
ww.National defense and military: National defense is paid from general federal revenue such as income taxes. FICA taxes are earmarked for Social Security and Medicare, not the military.
ww.Public schools and libraries: Public schools and libraries are funded largely by state and local taxes such as property taxes. FICA is a federal payroll tax for Social Security and Medicare.

rw: A deduction reduces taxable income, not the tax directly. At a 22 percent bracket, $1,000 times 0.22 gives $220 of tax saved.

ww.$780: $780 is what remains of the $1,000 after paying the 22 percent. A deduction saves tax equal to the deduction times the rate, not the leftover.
ww.$1,000: A $1,000 saving would only occur with a credit. A deduction lowers taxable income, so the tax saved is $1,000 times 22 percent, which is $220.
ww.$22: $22 would be 22 percent of $100. A $1,000 deduction at a 22 percent bracket saves $1,000 times 0.22, which is $220, not $22.

rw: A tax credit reduces the tax owed dollar for dollar, so a $1,000 credit cuts the tax bill by the full $1,000, unlike a deduction that lowers income.

ww.$0: A credit does reduce tax. A $0 reduction would ignore that a credit lowers the tax bill dollar for dollar, so $1,000 of credit saves $1,000.
ww.$220: $220 is the saving from a $1,000 deduction at a 22 percent bracket. A credit works directly on the tax owed, so it saves the full $1,000.
ww.$100: $100 would be 10 percent of the credit. A credit reduces the tax owed by its full value, so a $1,000 credit saves $1,000.

rw: Withholding is income tax that employers take out of each paycheck and send to the government on the worker's behalf, as a prepayment of the tax owed for the year.

ww.A savings plan at work offered by employ: A savings plan at work is a retirement plan like a 401(k). Withholding is tax taken out of pay, not a savings program offered by employers.
ww.A fee charged by the bank for cashing a: Banks may charge fees for cashing checks, but that is not withholding. Withholding is the tax an employer takes from pay and sends to the government.
ww.Money an employer keeps from the paychec: Employers send withheld money to the government and do not keep it. Withholding is a tax payment, not a bonus for the employer.

rw: A large refund means more tax was taken from paychecks than was owed, so the government returns the extra. It is effectively an interest-free loan to the government.

ww.Taxes do not apply to refunds in any yea: Refunds are not taxes. The refund is the return of overpaid tax, so saying taxes do not apply to refunds misses what it indicates about withholding.
ww.No tax was withheld during the year by t: If no tax were withheld, the worker would likely owe tax at filing and not receive a refund. A large refund shows too much was withheld.
ww.Too little tax was withheld from paychec: Too little withholding would produce a balance due when filing, not a refund. A large refund shows the opposite, which is that too much was withheld.

rw: The student should check whether income requires a return and whether filing could produce a refund. With $0 withheld, no refund is likely, but filing may still be needed.

ww.Nothing, since students never file tax r: Students do not automatically avoid filing. Whether a return is required depends on income and filing status, and filing may be needed to claim refunds.
ww.Whether the employer is a nonprofit grou: Whether the employer is a nonprofit or a for-profit firm does not decide filing duties. The worker's income, status and withholding matter instead.
ww.Let their employer file for them, as the: Employers do not file returns for workers. They report wages on a W-2, but each person must file their own return if required or to claim a refund.

rw: With no withholding, a freelancer must pay estimated taxes during the year, plus self-employment tax of 15.3 percent for Social Security and Medicare on net earnings.

ww.Paying tax only if the freelancer wishes: Paying tax is not optional. Self-employment income is taxable and must be reported, and ignoring it can bring penalties and interest from the tax authority.
ww.A refund automatically, as freelancers a: Freelancers are self-employed, not employees, so no employer withholds tax. A refund does not come automatically, and they usually owe tax at filing.
ww.Nothing, because freelance income is tax: Freelance income is taxable like other income. Saying it is tax free is false, and ignoring it can lead to penalties for underpayment.

rw: Self-employed people pay self-employment tax themselves, covering both the employer and employee halves of Social Security and Medicare, since there is no employer to share it.

ww.The government alone: The government does not pay self-employment tax for workers. It collects the tax from the self-employed person, who must pay both the employer and employee share.
ww.Their customers, who pay it: Customers pay for the work, but they do not pay the freelancer's self-employment tax. The self-employed person must calculate and pay it on their own net earnings.
ww.Their suppliers or buyers: Suppliers and buyers have no legal duty to pay a self-employed person's tax. The obligation rests on the self-employed worker, who reports and pays it.

rw: Form 1040 is the standard federal individual income tax return, where taxpayers report income, claim deductions and credits, and calculate the tax owed or the refund due.

ww.A form used to report payments to contra: Reporting payments to contractors is done with Form 1099-NEC. Form 1040 is the individual return filed by taxpayers, not an information form.
ww.A form used to set withholding at work e: Setting withholding at work is done with Form W-4. Form 1040 is filed at tax time to report income and compute tax owed.
ww.A form used by employers to report wages: Employers report wages to employees on Form W-2. Form 1040 is the return that individuals file themselves, not an employer's wage report.

rw: The usual deadline for most individual federal returns is April 15, moving to the next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday.

ww.January 1, at the start of the year: January 1 is the start of the tax year, and returns for the prior year are not due then. Most filers have until mid-April.
ww.July 4, the national holiday day: July 4 is a holiday with no link to tax filing. The standard deadline is April 15, though extensions can move it later.
ww.December 31, the last day of the year: December 31 ends the tax year, but returns are filed afterward. The deadline for most individuals falls on April 15 of the following year.

rw: A tax bracket is a range of taxable income that is taxed at a particular rate. The US system has several brackets, with higher rates on higher slices of income.

ww.A fee for filing a tax return late, adde: A fee for filing late is a late-filing penalty. A bracket is a range of income taxed at one rate, not a charge for lateness.
ww.A form used to claim a refund from the s: A form used to claim a refund is a return. A tax bracket is a range of income, and it has nothing to do with claiming refunds.
ww.A type of tax-exempt bond issued by citi: Tax-exempt bonds issued by cities are municipal bonds. A tax bracket is an income range with a rate, not a type of bond.

rw: The system is marginal, so only income inside the higher bracket is taxed at the higher rate. Income below stays at lower rates, so a raise never lowers take-home pay.

ww.You must pay back your raise to the gove: You never have to pay back a raise because of brackets. Only the extra income above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate, so you still gain.
ww.Your taxes drop on all of your income fo: A raise does not lower taxes on all income. The portion moved into a higher bracket is taxed more, so total tax usually rises with income.
ww.All of your income is taxed at the highe: Not all income is taxed at the higher rate. Brackets are marginal, so each slice of income is taxed at its own rate and lower slices stay the same.

rw: A use tax is owed on goods bought out of state, such as online, when no sales tax was charged, so it matches the sales tax you would have paid at home.

ww.A tax on using public roads, paid when d: Taxes on fuel for road use are excise taxes collected at the pump. A use tax applies to goods bought elsewhere and used in your own state.
ww.A tax on using the internet at home or a: There is no general tax for using the internet at home or at an office. A use tax applies to purchased goods brought into the state.
ww.A tax on using a library at a school or: A library or a school does not charge a use tax. This kind of tax applies to goods bought out of state and used within your own state.

rw: An excise tax is charged on specific goods or activities, such as gasoline, tobacco, alcohol and airline tickets, and is often built into the price you pay.

ww.A tax on investments held by firms and s: A tax on investments held by firms and savers is a capital or income tax, not an excise tax. Excise taxes apply to particular goods and services.
ww.A tax on the sale of homes by owners eac: A tax on the sale of homes is a transfer or capital gains tax. An excise tax is levied on specific goods or activities, not home sales.
ww.A tax on all income earned by workers an: A tax on all income of workers and firms is an income tax. An excise tax targets particular products, not broad earnings.

rw: An estate tax is charged on the transfer of a deceased person's property to heirs, and in the US applies only to estates above a high exemption amount.

ww.A tax on selling a home or other real es: A tax on selling a home is a capital gains or transfer tax. An estate tax is triggered by death and applies to the property left behind.
ww.A tax on rental income earned by a landl: A tax on rental income is an income tax paid by the landlord. An estate tax applies to inherited wealth, not to income earned from rentals.
ww.A tax on buying real estate, paid at clo: A tax paid when buying real estate is a transfer or recording tax at closing. An estate tax is about passing property after death.

rw: A capital gains tax is charged on the profit you make when you sell an asset, such as stocks or property, for more than you paid for it.

ww.A tax on interest paid on a savings acco: A tax on interest paid by a bank is income tax on interest. A capital gains tax applies to profit from selling an asset, not to interest.
ww.A tax on gifts given to others by one pe: A tax on gifts is a gift tax. Capital gains tax applies when an asset such as stock or property is sold for more than it cost.
ww.A tax on wages and salaries paid to work: A tax on wages and salaries is an income or payroll tax. Capital gains tax applies to profit from selling assets, not to earnings from work.

rw: Tax law gives lower rates to gains on assets held longer than a year, which encourages long-term investing, while short-term gains are taxed at ordinary income rates.

ww.Short-term gains are never taxed at the: Short-term gains are taxed, at ordinary income rates. Saying they are never taxed at the federal level is false, and the real difference is in the rates.
ww.Long-term gains are always tax-free, wha: Long-term gains are not tax-free, since they are taxed at rates of 0, 15 or 20 percent depending on income. Only some low-income filers pay zero.
ww.The rates are the same for both types of: The rates differ. Short-term gains are taxed at ordinary income rates, while long-term gains get lower special rates, so saying they are the same is wrong.

rw: A tax-exempt organization, such as a charity, church or school, is recognized by law as not required to pay certain taxes, like federal income tax, on activities tied to its mission.

ww.A business that pays no taxes of any kin: Tax-exempt groups are not free of all taxes. They may still pay payroll taxes, and taxes on unrelated business income, so saying any kind is overstated.
ww.A government office that sells bonds to: A government office selling bonds is a government agency or issuer. A tax-exempt organization is a nonprofit entity recognized by law, not a bond seller.
ww.A company that is too small to pay tax o: Small size alone does not make a company exempt. Businesses owe tax on income whatever their size, while exempt status depends on legal qualification as a nonprofit.

rw: Without payment or an extension, unpaid tax accrues late-payment penalties and interest, so you owe more over time. Filing an extension does not extend the time to pay.

ww.You receive a bonus refund anyway: Underpaying brings a bill, not a bonus. Nobody receives a refund for tax they failed to pay, so this outcome is the opposite of what happens.
ww.The debt is erased by the tax agency: Tax debts are not erased by the agency. The amount stays owed, and penalties and interest grow until it is paid or settled by a formal process.
ww.Nothing, as the agency does not check: The tax agency does check returns through matching and audits. Assuming nothing happens is a risky mistake, since unpaid tax is eventually discovered and charged.

rw: Itemizing makes sense when your allowed expenses, such as mortgage interest, state taxes and charity, add up to more than the standard deduction, which lowers taxable income further.

ww.When they have no receipts to claim at a: Without receipts, a taxpayer cannot support itemized deductions, and the standard deduction is the better choice. Having no records is a reason not to itemize.
ww.When they have no expenses to claim at a: With no expenses to claim, itemizing gives a deduction of zero, so the standard deduction is clearly better. Itemizing helps only when expenses are large.
ww.When they want to pay more tax, so they: Itemizing lowers taxable income and reduces tax, so wanting to pay more tax is no reason. The choice should depend on which deduction is larger.

rw: A W-9 is the form an independent contractor gives a business, listing their name, address and taxpayer identification number so the business can report payments on Form 1099.

ww.A form employees use to set withholding: Employees use a W-4 to set withholding at a new job. A W-9 is for contractors and has nothing to do with withholding choices.
ww.A form that shows an employee's yearly w: The form showing an employee's yearly wages and tax withheld is a W-2. A W-9 supplies a contractor's taxpayer information instead.
ww.A form to request an extension of the ta: An extension of the filing date is requested with Form 4868. A W-9 gives a contractor's taxpayer details to a business, not a request to the IRS.

rw: Form 1099-NEC reports payments of $600 or more made to independent contractors and other non-employees, so the payee can report the income and pay tax on it.

ww.Reporting stock sales and gains on trade: Reporting stock sales and gains uses Form 1099-B, issued by brokers. A 1099-NEC reports non-employee pay such as fees paid to contractors.
ww.Reporting wages to employees at year end: Wages paid to employees are reported on Form W-2. A 1099-NEC is used for non-employees, so reporting wages to employees is the wrong form.
ww.Reporting a gift made to a family member: Gifts are not reported on this form. Large gifts may need a gift tax return, Form 709, but 1099-NEC concerns payments for services by non-employees.

rw: Earned income is money from working, including wages, salaries, tips and net self-employment income. It is the basis for credits like the EITC and for IRA contributions.

ww.Money from interest and dividends only,: Interest and dividends are investment income, which is not earned income. Earned income comes from working, so this answer leaves out wages and self-employment pay.
ww.Money from selling a car at a profit to: Profit from selling a car is a capital gain, not pay for work. Earned income comes from working, such as wages or self-employment, not from asset sales.
ww.Money from gifts given by relatives and: Gifts from relatives are not earned, since no work was done to receive them. Earned income arises from labor, such as wages or running a business.

rw: Passive income comes from activities needing little day-to-day effort, such as rental property or limited partnerships. It differs from wages because ongoing work is not required.

ww.A tax refund from the government after t: A tax refund returns overpaid tax and is not income from an activity. Passive income is money earned from sources such as rentals with little regular effort.
ww.Wages from a full-time job at a firm, pa: Wages from a full-time job are earned income because they require regular work. Passive income needs little ongoing effort, so wages do not qualify.
ww.Money received as a gift from relatives,: A gift is money received without work, but it is not passive income. Passive income comes from assets or businesses like rentals that earn money with little effort.

rw: A tax-advantaged account offers special tax treatment, such as deductible contributions or tax-free growth. Examples include IRAs, 401(k) plans, HSAs and 529 college savings plans.

ww.An account with no fees of any kind for: Fees can apply to tax-advantaged accounts. The term describes tax treatment, not fee levels, so saying there are no fees of any kind is wrong.
ww.An account that pays no interest on the: Tax-advantaged accounts generally do pay interest or earn returns. The advantage concerns taxes, not interest, so an account paying none does not fit.
ww.An account the government runs for citiz: An account run by the government for people without savings is a welfare program. A tax-advantaged account is open to savers and has special tax treatment.

rw: Money works as a medium of exchange for buying goods, a unit of account for pricing them, and a store of value that holds purchasing power over time.

ww.Spending, borrowing and lending of money: Spending, borrowing and lending are uses of money, not its functions. The three functions are medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value.
ww.Only a way to decorate a wallet, with li: Money is a practical economic tool and not decoration. Its real functions are exchange, measuring value and storing value, so this answer is not a function.
ww.Saving, investing and taxing of money by: Saving, investing and taxing are activities involving money, not its functions. Money itself serves as a medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value.

rw: Inflation is a general, sustained rise in the overall price level over time, which reduces what each dollar can buy. It is usually measured by an index like CPI.

ww.A rise in the price of one item only: A rise in the price of one item is a relative price change. Inflation means prices rise broadly across the economy, not for a single product.
ww.A rise in wages only, not prices: Rising wages alone are not inflation. Inflation refers to a general rise in prices, though wages and prices may move together at times.
ww.A general fall in prices over time: A general fall in prices over time is deflation, the opposite of inflation. Inflation means prices rise on average across the economy.

rw: Prices rose faster than pay, 3 percent versus 2 percent, so your pay buys fewer goods than before. Your real income fell by about 1 percent.

ww.No change: Buying power changes when prices and pay grow at different rates. Prices rose 3 percent while pay rose only 2 percent, so there was a change.
ww.It doubled: Buying power cannot double when pay lags prices. Pay rose 2 percent against 3 percent price growth, so the effect is a small decline.
ww.It rose: Buying power rises only if pay grows faster than prices. Here pay rose 2 percent against 3 percent price growth, so it fell and did not rise.

rw: If prices double, each dollar buys only about half as many goods as before. Purchasing power falls in proportion to the rise in the price level.

ww.It buys twice as much now: If prices double, each dollar buys less, not more. Buying twice as much would require prices to fall by half instead.
ww.It buys the same amount: Doubled prices mean a dollar buys less. It cannot buy the same amount, because the same goods now cost twice as much.
ww.It becomes worthless at once: Money loses purchasing power but does not become worthless at once. A dollar still buys something, only about half as much if prices double.

rw: The CPI tracks the change in prices of a fixed basket of goods and services bought by typical urban consumers, and it is the standard gauge of inflation.

ww.A measure of interest rates charged by t: Interest rates charged by banks are measured by rate surveys, not CPI. CPI tracks the prices consumers pay, not borrowing costs.
ww.A measure of employment levels across th: Employment levels are measured by the unemployment rate and jobs reports. CPI measures price changes, not how many people hold jobs.
ww.A measure of the profits of companies, f: Company profits are reported in earnings statements. CPI follows consumer prices and is not a measure of corporate profit.

rw: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States. It sets monetary policy, supervises banks, and works to keep prices stable and employment high.

ww.A government agency that collects taxes: Collecting taxes is the job of the IRS and other revenue agencies. The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supervises banks instead.
ww.A stock exchange for trading shares: A stock exchange, such as the NYSE or Nasdaq, trades shares. The Federal Reserve does not run a market for shares but sets monetary policy.
ww.A commercial bank that lends for profit: The Fed does not operate to earn profit from lending. It acts as the central bank and as lender of last resort, with policy goals instead.

rw: When the Fed raises its rates, banks pay more to borrow, so loan rates on mortgages, cards and car loans tend to rise, and borrowing becomes more costly.

ww.They stay the same: Borrowing costs do not stay fixed when the Fed raises rates. Banks pass higher funding costs on, so consumer loan rates usually move upward in response.
ww.They tend to fall: Rates tend to fall when the Fed lowers rates, not raises them. A rise in the policy rate pushes loan rates up and makes borrowing costlier.
ww.They disappear: Borrowing costs never vanish when the Fed raises rates. Higher policy rates make loans more costly, and interest remains part of every loan.

rw: The real interest rate is the nominal rate minus the inflation rate. It shows the true gain in purchasing power that an investor earns, or the cost a borrower pays.

ww.The highest rate that a bank may charge: The highest rate a bank may charge is a usury cap, which is a legal limit. The real rate is a measure that adjusts for inflation.
ww.The rate printed on a loan agreement, un: The rate printed on a loan agreement is the nominal rate. The real rate corrects that figure for inflation, so unadjusted is the opposite meaning.
ww.The interest rate that applies to real e: A rate on real estate loans is a mortgage rate. The real interest rate is a different idea that accounts for inflation and has no link to property.

rw: The real rate is the nominal rate minus inflation, so 3 percent minus 2 percent equals about 1 percent. Your savings gain only a little buying power.

ww.About 0 percent: A real rate near zero would need inflation near 3 percent. With 2 percent inflation, the nominal 3 percent leaves about 1 percent after adjusting.
ww.About 6 percent: Six percent would come from adding 3 and 2 and then doubling the sum. The real rate subtracts inflation, giving 3 minus 2, or about 1 percent.
ww.About 5 percent: Five percent adds inflation to the nominal rate. Inflation erodes returns, so you subtract it, and 3 minus 2 gives a real rate near 1 percent.

rw: Liquidity describes how quickly an asset can be spent or turned into cash without losing much value. Cash and checking balances are highly liquid, while property is not.

ww.It is held in a bank account for savings: Holding money in a bank account does not define liquidity, since some bank accounts, such as long-term CDs, are hard to access without penalty.
ww.It never changes in value, whatever happ: Liquid money can change in value, as with shares that sell easily. Liquidity concerns how fast an asset becomes cash, not whether its value is stable.
ww.It is invested in stocks and bonds only: Stocks and bonds can be fairly liquid, but liquidity is not limited to them. It describes how fast any asset can be turned into cash.

rw: In a recession, businesses cut costs and lay off workers, so job losses and lower incomes become more likely for households, which strains budgets.

ww.Jobs become easier to find for most work: In a recession jobs become harder to find, not easier. Employers cut hiring while many people search for work, so this answer reverses the effect.
ww.Prices fall to zero, so households buy g: Prices do not fall to zero in a recession. Some prices fall or rise more slowly, but goods are never free, and households still must pay.
ww.Wages always rise for all workers in the: Wages do not always rise in a recession. Pay often stagnates or is cut and hours are reduced, so this claim is false for most workers.
